十四世紀伊本·白圖泰提及女性彈撥弓形樂器，或為科拉琴早期線索，但不足以確認。曼丁: In the fourteenth century Ibn Battuta mentions a bowed string instrument played by women, which may be an early trace of the kora but is not enough to confirm it. Mande oral tradition says it came from Kabu, that Jali Mady Wuleng Sisoko bought it from a spirit and first played “Kelefaba”. Mungo Park's book of 1799 leaves the earliest European account, and the instrument later appears in the national anthem of Senegal. The end of the twentieth century brought twenty-five-string and double-neck versions; monks at the Keur Moussa monastery may have introduced guitar tuning pegs, and Dominique Catta taught it from notation. Robert Grawi also built the gravikord and the gravikola for modern performance.

演奏科拉琴以手指撥弦發聲，傳統風格用雙手同時撥出多聲節奏型，其餘手指握住弦兩側的: The kora is played by plucking the strings with the fingers; in the traditional style both hands pluck a polyphonic rhythmic pattern at once, while the remaining fingers grip the handles on either side of the strings to steady the instrument. A beginner can first learn how the left and right hands divide the eleven and the ten strings, then practise keeping a repeated pattern going while an improvised melody runs at the same time. To tune, the leather tuning rings are moved up and down to bring the instrument into one of four seven-note scales; traditional tuning is no easier than playing.

科拉琴常見於西非馬利、幾內亞、幾內亞比索與塞內加爾的賈利口傳場合，用於歷史、族譜: The kora is common on jeli oral occasions in Mali, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau and Senegal, where it is used for reciting history, genealogies and stories. Traditionally both hands pluck cross-rhythmic ostinati while an improvised solo runs at the same time; the sound is close to the harp, and it has also been likened to the plucking of flamenco or Delta blues. Today it appears in solo performance, in duos with Western instruments, in studio work and on jazz recordings; the national anthem of Senegal also mentions the kora.
科拉琴有二十一弦，每弦一音，可調成四種七聲音階。其聲音近似豎琴，但傳統演奏以雙手: The kora has twenty-one strings, one note to each, and can be tuned to four seven-note scales. Its sound is close to the harp, but the traditional way of playing plucks with both hands, so that a multi-rhythmic ostinato (kumbengo) and an improvised solo (birimintingo) go on at once, and it sounds close to flamenco or Delta blues guitar. The instrument has features of both lute and harp and belongs among the double-bridge harp lutes. Volume used to be reinforced by metal leaves, nyenmyemo, clamped to the bridge or the top of the neck; today an electronic pickup is more often used.
科拉琴琴身以葫蘆對半製成，上覆牛皮作共鳴箱；琴頸為硬木，皮面下方有兩支把手支撐。: The body of the kora is a gourd cut in half and covered with cowhide to make the resonator; the neck is hardwood, and two handles under the hide give it support. The strings were traditionally thin strips of cowhide or antelope hide; today harp strings or nylon fishing line are more often used, sometimes braided together to make them thicker. Leather tuning rings (konso) are moved up and down to tune, and some modern instruments use guitar-style pegs instead. The old resonator pieces (nyenmyemo) are of tin or brass, with metal coils threaded round their edges. The source does not state the materials of other parts such as the bridge and the handles.
科拉琴（Kora）是西非弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號323.2: The kora is a West African chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 323.2. Half a gourd covered with cowhide makes the resonator, joined to a long hardwood neck; twenty-one strings are plucked with the fingers and carried on two rows of free-standing bridges, so the instrument has features of both lute and harp and belongs among the double-bridge harp lutes. It is traditionally played by jeli families and is found in Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Mali and Senegal, and earliest in the Gambia.
